stories.headline: OCTOBER HIKE ODDS HIT 71% AS FED PIVOTS FROM CUTS TO HIKES
stories.body: CME FedWatch odds of a second-straight rate hike at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting rose to 71%, up from 66% a day earlier and just 8.8% a month ago. The Fed already raised its target range 25 bps to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16 in its first hike since 2023, with 16 of 18 policymakers penciling in at least one more before year-end.
stories.explain: A rate hike two meetings in a row, arriving months after the Fed was still cutting, means the committee sees inflation re-accelerating faster than growth is slowing — exactly the scenario that forces central banks to reverse course quickly. Because Fed funds futures reprice continuously between meetings, that 71% probability already flows straight into every other yield on the curve well before October 28, which is why bond and equity markets are responding today rather than waiting three weeks.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 19-YEAR HIGH, 30-YEAR TOPS LEVELS UNSEEN SINCE 2004
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at 5.17%, a whisker below Thursday's 19-year high, while the 30-year sits near 5.50%, its highest since 2004, and the 2-year holds around 4.80%. The pause follows a week-long selloff driven by hawkish Fed commentary, elevated energy prices, and a hot PMI report.
stories.explain: Long yields stalling rather than reversing signals the market isn't fighting the repriced hike path — it's digesting it. The 30-year's move is the more telling one: it's driven mostly by term premium (compensation for holding duration risk) rather than near-term Fed expectations, so its rise to a 22-year high reflects investors demanding more compensation for uncertainty about where inflation and deficits land over the next three decades, not just where rates sit next quarter.

stories.headline: DOW JUMPS 478 POINTS, STOCKS NOTCH WEEKLY GAINS DESPITE BOND SELLOFF
stories.body: The Dow rose 478.64 points (+0.93%) to 51,828.62, the S&P 500 gained 0.51% to 7,743.41, and the Nasdaq added 0.5%, with all three snapping the Dow's three-week losing streak on a weekly basis (S&P +0.7%, Nasdaq +1.6%) as oil prices eased and the Treasury selloff paused.
stories.explain: Equities rallying on the same day yields merely stopped rising — rather than needing yields to actually fall — shows how much of this month's stock weakness was a rate-of-change story: markets sell off hardest while repricing is happening, then stabilize once the new hike odds are fully absorbed into prices, even if the absolute yield level stays elevated.

stories.headline: OIL SLIDES 2.2% AS SUPPLY FEARS EASE, TAKING PRESSURE OFF STOCKS
stories.body: WTI crude fell 2.2% to $92.55 a barrel Friday, its first meaningful pullback after a month-long, 40%-plus run driven largely by the Iran-linked Strait of Hormuz standoff, giving equity markets room to rally as one of the two big macro headwinds this week (oil and yields) finally loosened its grip.
stories.explain: Crude carries a geopolitical risk premium on top of physical supply-and-demand fundamentals whenever a chokepoint like Hormuz is contested, and that premium can compress quickly on any de-escalation signal even without a change in actual barrels flowing. Lower oil also feeds directly into headline CPI, so today's pullback modestly eases the same inflation math that's been pushing the Fed toward more hikes.

stories.headline: CONSUMER SENTIMENT SINKS TO 48.1 AS INFLATION EXPECTATIONS JUMP TO 4.6%
stories.body: The University of Michigan's final September sentiment index fell to 48.1 from August's 51.7 (-7% month-over-month) and 12.7% below year-ago levels, while the one-year inflation outlook climbed to 4.6% from 4.0% in August — its steepest reading since June, even as it beat the preliminary 47.8 print.
stories.explain: The Fed treats this survey's inflation-expectations component as an early-warning gauge for whether the public is starting to 'de-anchor' — building rising prices into their own wage demands and spending decisions, which can turn a temporary price shock into a self-reinforcing spiral. A jump like today's 60-bp rise, layered on top of an already-hawkish Fed, is precisely the kind of data point that hardens the case for the October hike the futures market is now pricing at 71%.

stories.headline: NEVADA'S STEVE ALFORD TO RETIRE AS ELIGIBILITY AND INJURY NEWS PILE UP
stories.body: Nevada head coach Steve Alford announced he'll retire at season's end after 36 years on the bench. Elsewhere, Roddy Gayle Jr. won a court case in New York securing a fifth year of eligibility, while Michigan freshman guard Brandon McCoy Jr. tore his ACL in an exhibition game in Montenegro and will miss the season.

stories.headline: GRIZZLIES WAIVE D'ANGELO RUSSELL IN ROSTER CRUNCH AHEAD OF CAMP
stories.body: Memphis waived D'Angelo Russell Friday after entering camp with 19 players on standard deals against a 15-man roster limit. Dallas held its media day, previewing a Kyrie Irving-Cooper Flagg pairing under new coach and GM structure; veterans report September 28 with camps opening league-wide September 29.

stories.headline: QB INJURY WAVE RESHAPES WEEK 3 AS DANIELS, DART SIDELINED
stories.body: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels will miss Sunday's home game against Seattle after redislocating his elbow, handing the start to Marcus Mariota, while Jaxson Dart's injury has thrust Jameis Winston back into the Giants' lineup — both teams now face 2027-draft QB questions. Elsewhere, the 49ers are 2-0 with 62 points and zero sacks allowed on Brock Purdy.

stories.headline: NO. 1 TEXAS AT NO. 14 TENNESSEE HEADLINES STACKED WEEK 4 SATURDAY
stories.body: Week 4 opened Friday night with No. 5 Indiana hosting Northwestern in Bloomington, chasing a third straight shutout, before Saturday's marquee slate: No. 1 Texas at No. 14 Tennessee, No. 4 Ole Miss at No. 21 Florida, and Colorado at Baylor among the featured games.

sports.detail: Beat Eastern Washington 48-16 last week. Next: vs. Minnesota, Saturday Sept. 26, 8:00 PM PT at Husky Stadium (FOX) — the Big Ten opener and first meeting since 1977.
Added Texas Tech transfer guard LeJuan Watts (11.8 ppg last season) and Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno to the backcourt. Season opens with a WSU exhibition Oct. 25.
Beat the Cardinals 31-7 last week. Next: at Commanders, Sunday Sept. 27, 10:00 AM PT — Washington will start Marcus Mariota after Jayden Daniels redislocated his elbow.
Signed Ausar Thompson to a 5-year extension through 2031-32; talks with Jalen Duren remain stalled roughly $5M/year apart. Training camp opens Sept. 29.
Officially eliminated from playoff contention Thursday as Texas beat the Mets; fell to the Angels 6-4 (Julio Rodríguez homered). Season-closing series continues tonight, 6:40 PM PT, T-Mobile Park.

deepDive.title: Why the Fed Watches a Consumer Survey: Inflation Expectations and the De-Anchoring Risk
content: Today's brief contains an odd pairing: consumer sentiment just sank to 48.1, one of the weakest readings in modern history, yet the same data release is part of why futures markets pushed October hike odds to 71%. That's not a contradiction — it's because the Fed isn't just watching how people feel about the economy, it's watching one specific sub-component of that survey: what people expect inflation to do over the next year. That expectations gauge jumped to 4.6% from 4.0% in a single month, and it is arguably more important to the Fed's next move than the headline sentiment number itself.

The mechanism is called expectations anchoring. If households and firms believe inflation will stay near the Fed's 2% target, they set wages, prices, and contracts accordingly, which helps inflation actually land near target — a self-fulfilling stability. But if expectations start drifting upward, workers demand bigger raises to protect purchasing power, businesses pass through costs more readily since they expect competitors to do the same, and the economy can slide into a wage-price spiral that persists even after the original shock (in this case, energy prices tied to the Hormuz standoff) fades. The University of Michigan survey is one of the Fed's most-cited real-time gauges of whether that drift is happening.

This is precisely the lesson of the 1970s, when the Fed under Arthur Burns treated rising inflation expectations as noise rather than signal, let them become entrenched, and needed Paul Volcker's brutal early-1980s hikes — with the fed funds rate above 19% — to break the spiral. Modern Fed officials, including those advocating for today's hikes, explicitly cite that history: they would rather over-tighten now, even against weak sentiment and a slowing economy, than risk a repeat de-anchoring that takes years and a recession to reverse. That's the reasoning behind hiking into a sentiment reading this poor.

For markets, it means the University of Michigan release on the first Friday of every month deserves as much attention as CPI itself, since a further rise in that 4.6% expectations figure would very plausibly push October's hike odds well past 71%, while a reversal back toward 4.0% would give the Fed room to pause. Watch whether next month's preliminary reading, due in early October, extends this jump — it will likely move Fed funds futures more than most scheduled economic data between now and the October 27-28 meeting.
